objectives: Recognize when threads vs processes is the right choice.

slides.title: Process vs thread, precisely
slides.body:
**Process**: an instance of a running program. Has its own address space (virtual memory), file descriptors, signal handlers, working directory. Created by `fork()` (Unix) or `CreateProcess()` (Windows). Isolated from other processes — a buggy process can't (directly) corrupt another.

**Thread**: a unit of execution within a process. Shares the process's address space, file descriptors, etc. with other threads. Created by `pthread_create()` / `std::thread` / language-level abstractions. Lighter than processes (no address-space setup); communication via shared memory.

The trade-off:
- **Processes**: heavyweight (~1ms to fork), strong isolation, IPC via pipes/sockets.
- **Threads**: cheap (~10µs to create), shared memory, no isolation (one thread's bug can corrupt others).

Production patterns:
- **Multi-process**: Chrome (process-per-tab for isolation), Postgres (process-per-connection historically), Apache pre-fork.
- **Multi-thread**: most modern application servers, JVMs, the kernel itself.

The Python GIL + Ruby GVL famously limit thread parallelism in those languages, pushing CPU-bound work back to multi-process (multiprocessing module).

slides.title: fork() + copy-on-write
slides.body:
Unix `fork()` creates a child process that's an exact copy of the parent — same code, same memory, same file descriptors. Implementing this naively (copy all the parent's memory) would be slow.

**Copy-on-write (COW)**: at fork time, parent + child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. When either tries to write, the kernel takes a page fault, copies that page, and lets the write proceed on the private copy.

Result: fork() is cheap if the child immediately calls `exec()` (loads a new program → discards all parent's pages). The classic `fork() + exec()` pattern (your shell launching a command) leverages this — the parent's memory is never actually copied.

**Subtle trap**: COW interacts with multi-threading. `fork()` in a multi-threaded process only carries the calling thread to the child; locks held by other threads remain locked in the child but their holders don't exist there. POSIX says: `fork()` after threads = only call async-signal-safe functions in the child until `exec()`. Most languages avoid this entirely by spawning processes via posix_spawn or vfork instead.

slides.title: The C10K problem + modern alternatives
slides.body:
**C10K**: the early-2000s challenge of handling 10,000 concurrent connections per server. Thread-per-connection didn't scale: 10K threads ≈ 8GB of stack memory alone (default 8MB stack × 10K threads). Plus kernel scheduling overhead.

**Solutions** that emerged:
- **Event-driven I/O** (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD): one thread handles thousands of connections via non-blocking I/O + an event loop. Nginx, Node.js, Redis.
- **Coroutines / green threads**: lightweight user-space threads. Go's goroutines (~2KB stack, multiplexed onto OS threads), Rust async, Python asyncio.
- **io_uring** (Linux 5.1+): submission/completion queues for batched async I/O. Lower per-syscall overhead than epoll for very high-IOPS workloads.

Production reality: modern servers handle millions of concurrent connections via coroutines + event loops. The thread-per-connection model is dead for high-concurrency networking.

question.question: Derive fork() time complexity with COW
question.goal: Process has $N$ pages of memory. Without COW, fork copies all $N$. With COW, what's the immediate cost + the eventual cost?

steps.prompt: Immediate cost: mark all $N$ pages COW (no actual copying). Page table walk only. What's the complexity?
hints: Page table modification is $O(N)$ in pages.
steps.reveal: $O(N)$ immediate — touching every page-table entry to mark COW.

steps.prompt: If child writes to $W$ pages before calling exec(), what's the additional cost?
steps.motivation: Each write to COW page triggers a fault + copy.
steps.reveal: $O(W)$ additional. If child immediately execs, $W = 0$ — fork is essentially free for the fork+exec pattern.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{fork: } O(N + W) \text{ where } W \text{ = pages written before exec}}$$ For `fork() + exec()`, $W \approx 0$, so cost is dominated by the page-table walk. Modern Linux: ~1ms for fork on a 100MB process; ~10µs for the eventual write copies if any.

question.question: Building a web server with ~10,000 concurrent connections. Each connection mostly waits on I/O. Best architecture:
options: Event-driven I/O with a small thread pool (e.g., Node.js, Go goroutines, async Python/Rust).
question.explanation: 10K threads = 80GB of stack memory + kernel scheduling overhead. Event-driven I/O multiplexes all 10K connections onto a small thread pool (often 1 thread per CPU core); each connection is just a small state-machine struct. Node.js, Go (goroutines + epoll), Nginx, modern Python asyncio all use this model.

hints: How much memory would 10K threads consume just in stacks?
Mostly-idle connections don't benefit from dedicated threads.
slides.workedSolution: 10K threads × 8MB default stack = 80GB just for stacks. Each thread is also tracked by the kernel scheduler — switching among 10K threads has overhead even when most are idle. Event-driven I/O keeps just one or a few threads (= CPU cores) and a small per-connection state struct (~few KB). Modern servers (Cloudflare, Nginx, Node) handle millions of concurrent connections per node this way.

question.prompt: You have a Python program that needs to crunch numbers across 16 CPU cores. A teammate proposes using the `threading` module. Walk through why that's the wrong call + which Python concurrency primitive is right.
Explain in two or three sentences why most modern high-concurrency servers (Nginx, Node.js, Go) use event-driven I/O instead of thread-per-connection.
question.rubric: Mentions that 10K+ threads exhaust memory + kernel scheduling capacity; event-driven I/O multiplexes connections onto few threads via epoll/kqueue/io_uring; per-connection state is a small struct, not a heavyweight thread.
